pages.text: Eyram’s village grew good vegetables, but only one buyer came to collect them. He set the price for everyone, and nobody could argue. “Take it or leave it,” he would say, and the vegetables would soften in the sun. Eyram told her agriculture teacher, Mr Dadzie, at the Young Farmers Club. “Sir, why must one man decide the price for the whole village?” she asked. Mr Dadzie smiled. “Let me tell you about Anand,” he said.

“Sir, why must one man decide the price for the whole village?” she asked.
Mr Dadzie smiled.
“Let me tell you about Anand,” he said.
pages.alt: A girl with a basket of vegetables stands in front of a buyer’s pickup truck.

pages.text: “Anand is a town in Gujarat, in India,” said Mr Dadzie. “In the 1940s, small milk farmers in the Kaira area sold milk to agents. According to an encyclopaedia account, a private company had an effective monopoly, meaning it was the only buyer, on collecting milk from Kaira and supplying it to Mumbai. Prices were set arbitrarily. In 1946, the farmers formed a cooperative so that they could sell directly. It was registered on 14 December 1946 as the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers’ Union.”
sentences: “Anand is a town in Gujarat, in India,” said Mr Dadzie.
“In the 1940s, small milk farmers in the Kaira area sold milk to agents.
According to an encyclopaedia account, a private company had an effective monopoly, meaning it was the only buyer, on collecting milk from Kaira and supplying it to Mumbai.
Prices were set arbitrarily.
In 1946, the farmers formed a cooperative so that they could sell directly.
It was registered on 14 December 1946 as the Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers’ Union.”
pages.alt: A teacher points to a map of India with a drawing of milk cans and a small town marked.

pages.text: “How did it work?” asked Yaw. Mr Dadzie drew three boxes. “In every village, the milk producers form a village society and elect the members who manage it. The village societies together form a district union, which collects, processes and transports the milk. The district unions together run a state federation that markets the products, led by elected representatives who hire professional managers. This three-level structure is called the Anand pattern. Its brand is called Amul.”

pages.alt: A teacher draws three boxes labelled village, district and state, linked by arrows.

pages.text: “Today, the same account reports 3.6 million milk producers,” said Mr Dadzie. “It also says that, under its leader, the farmer received the largest share of what the customer paid, but it gives no percentage, so I will not give one. And remember, it took decades. Anand did not become big in one year.” Eyram wrote: farmers own it, farmers elect leaders, professionals manage it, farmers get the biggest share. She added a question mark. “How do they keep it honest?” she asked.

She added a question mark.
“How do they keep it honest?” she asked.
pages.alt: A teacher points to a bar chart of producers growing over many years beside a milk can.

pages.text: “Good question,” said Mr Dadzie. “Cooperatives can fail. They fail when records are poor, when leaders are not honest, when members do not attend meetings, or when the group cannot sell what it makes. So rules, records and regular accounts matter as much as the idea. And Anand is not Ghana. Our crops, our laws and our markets are different. We borrow the lesson, which is that farmers can own the link that pays them, but we do not copy the whole plan.”

pages.text: The Young Farmers Club held a pretend meeting. Eyram was elected chairperson, Yaw secretary and another pupil treasurer. They wrote rules: every member would have one vote, all money would be recorded, accounts would be read aloud every month, and nobody would sell secretly outside the agreed price. Mr Dadzie reminded them to ask the district office responsible for cooperatives how a real society is registered, because he had not checked the current rules.

pages.text: Mr Dadzie then set a reported-speech task. “‘The farmers formed a cooperative in 1946,’ said Mr Dadzie,” he wrote, and the class changed it: Mr Dadzie said that the farmers had formed a cooperative in 1946. “‘We will elect our leaders,’ said Eyram.” Eyram said that they would elect their leaders. “‘Do you want to join?’ asked Yaw.” Yaw asked me whether I wanted to join. “‘I am attending the meeting tomorrow,’ said Eyram.” Eyram said that she was attending the meeting the next day.

pages.alt: A teacher writes three direct sentences and three reported ones on the board in two colours.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: in reported speech, remove the quotation marks, add “that” (or “if” or “whether” for yes-or-no questions), and move the verb one step back in time: will becomes would, am or is becomes was, and the simple past becomes the past perfect. Change pronouns and time words too: tomorrow becomes the next day, and today becomes that day. Check each sentence for sense before you hand in your work. The end.
